events.title: Rhapsody in Blue Premieres
events.blurb: A 25-year-old former Tin Pan Alley song-plugger's first major concert work — a one-movement concerto for piano and jazz band — premiered at a Manhattan concert hall advertised as "An Experiment in Modern Music." The piece's opening clarinet glissando, improvised in rehearsal as a joke, was left in. The concert had begun with banal novelty pieces; by the time the composer walked out to sit at the piano, the audience was dozing. He woke them up.
events.revealBlurb: February 12, 1924 — George Gershwin at Aeolian Hall, Manhattan. The bandleader was Paul Whiteman. The audience included Rachmaninoff, Stravinsky, Fritz Kreisler, and Sergei Rachmaninoff. United Airlines has used it as its ad music since 1987.

events.title: Dylan Goes Electric
events.blurb: A 24-year-old folk singer, backed by a ragged rhythm section from the previous night's acquaintance, walked onto the stage of a folk festival on a Rhode Island pier with a sunburst Stratocaster slung low over his shoulder. He played three short electric songs before some boos drowned out the applause. He walked off, returned with his acoustic, and played two more. The event marked, depending on who tells it, the birth of folk-rock or the betrayal of American folk.
events.revealBlurb: July 25, 1965 — Bob Dylan at the Newport Folk Festival. Pete Seeger, legend says, tried to cut the sound cables with an axe. Seeger later denied it. The songs included "Maggie's Farm" and "Like a Rolling Stone." Dylan's next tour was booed nightly for a year.

events.title: Hip-Hop Born in the Bronx
events.blurb: An 18-year-old Jamaican-born DJ, using two turntables to extend the instrumental breaks of funk and soul records, played his younger sister's back-to-school party in the rec room of a public housing building in the South Bronx. His technique of looping drum breaks became the foundation of hip-hop. The party went so well that he began DJ-ing at local parks and block parties; rappers (then called MCs) began performing over his sets. A new culture was born.
events.revealBlurb: August 11, 1973 — DJ Kool Herc (Clive Campbell) at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue, the Bronx. The address is now a national historic site. Herc's "merry-go-round" technique of using two copies of the same record to loop the break is still the foundation of every hip-hop DJ set.

events.title: John Lennon Shot
events.blurb: A 40-year-old former Beatle, returning to his Manhattan apartment building with his wife after a late-night recording session, was shot four times in the back at close range by a young man he had signed an autograph for earlier that afternoon. He was pronounced dead at a nearby hospital 20 minutes later. Vigils were held around the world. His wife asked that his birthday be celebrated with international moments of silence, which has since become a yearly tradition.
events.revealBlurb: December 8, 1980 — John Lennon at The Dakota, NYC. Shooter Mark David Chapman remains in prison, denied parole 13 times. Lennon's album "Double Fantasy" had been released three weeks earlier; it took on enormous posthumous sales.

events.title: MTV Launches
events.blurb: A new American cable channel devoted entirely to music videos went on the air at one minute past midnight Eastern time with a countdown, a rocket, and a footage loop of the Apollo 11 moon landing with the channel's logo hoisted as a flag. The first music video it played was a novelty track by a British synth-pop group with a prescient title. Within four years it had reshaped the music industry's priorities and, quite possibly, a generation's attention span.
events.revealBlurb: August 1, 1981 — Music Television. First video: "Video Killed the Radio Star" by the Buggles. The channel ran music videos almost exclusively until the late 1990s; today it runs reality programming and airs barely any music.

events.title: First Website Goes Live
events.blurb: The first webpage to be publicly accessible on the internet was posted from a workstation in a Swiss laboratory. It explained what the World Wide Web was, how to set up a web server, and how to use a web browser. Its URL ended in ".ch"; its creator had built the whole stack — browser, server, editor, protocol — in about a year and a half.
events.revealBlurb: August 6, 1991 — info.cern.ch, by Tim Berners-Lee. The original page was lost at one point; CERN restored a 1992 copy in 2013. The server, a NeXT workstation, is still on display with a sticker reading "DO NOT POWER DOWN — THIS IS A SERVER."

events.title: Netscape IPO
events.blurb: A 16-month-old Silicon Valley company that had distributed free web browsers and had never turned a profit went public at $28 a share, opened at $71, and closed its first trading day at $58.25. Its 24-year-old co-founder was suddenly worth $58 million on paper. Wall Street had discovered the internet, and the next five years of stock-market mania had a starting gun.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 1995 — Netscape Communications. Co-founder Marc Andreessen ended up on the cover of Time two years later with the caption "The Kid Who Tamed the Web." Microsoft's bundled Internet Explorer would eventually kill Netscape; the company sold to AOL in 1999.

events.title: Napster Launched
events.blurb: A 19-year-old Northeastern University student released a peer-to-peer file-sharing program that let any user share their digitized music collection with any other user, anywhere in the world. Within 18 months, 80 million registered users were trading tens of millions of MP3 files a day. The recording industry sued; one rock band's lead drummer famously delivered a list of his fans using the service to Napster's offices in person.
events.revealBlurb: June 1, 1999 — Shawn Fanning. The suing drummer was Lars Ulrich of Metallica. Napster was shut down by a 2001 court ruling; the brand was later bought, sold, and reused several times, most recently by Algorand.

events.title: YouTube Launched
events.blurb: Three former PayPal employees, reportedly frustrated that they couldn't easily share a video of a dinner party or (by an alternate legend) a wardrobe malfunction from a recent sporting event, registered a domain name for a video-sharing site. The site's first uploaded video, "Me at the zoo," was an 18-second clip of one of the founders standing in front of elephants at the San Diego Zoo. Google bought them for $1.65 billion in stock twenty months later.
events.revealBlurb: February 14, 2005 — Chad Hurley, Steve Chen, Jawed Karim. The "Me at the zoo" video is still online, with over 350 million views. Users now upload over 500 hours of video every minute.

events.title: TikTok Launches Globally
events.blurb: A Chinese short-video company merged its existing lip-sync-focused app Musical.ly, acquired the previous year, into a new global brand — effectively introducing mainland China's most popular short-video format to Western audiences. The app's algorithm would prove uniquely good at inferring what content users wanted without asking them. Within three years, TikTok had over a billion users and had reshaped every other social platform's product roadmap.
events.revealBlurb: August 2, 2018 — ByteDance merges Musical.ly into TikTok. By 2020, U.S. users were spending more time per day in TikTok than in Instagram or Facebook. President Trump attempted to ban it in 2020; the Biden administration attempted to force a U.S. divestment in 2024.

events.title: Jesse Owens Wins First Berlin Gold
events.blurb: An American sprinter from Alabama won the first of four gold medals at the Berlin Summer Games, finishing the 100-metre dash in 10.3 seconds before 110,000 spectators. He went on to win gold in the 200 metres, long jump, and 4×100-metre relay — shattering the narrative that the host nation's athletes would dominate.

events.title: Jesse Owens at Berlin Olympics
events.blurb: A 22-year-old African-American sprinter won four gold medals at a Summer Olympics held in the capital of a regime that had publicly declared the inferiority of his race. He took the 100m (10.3), 200m (20.7), long jump (8.06m), and 4×100m relay. His performance personally refuted Nazi racial theorizing on a stage the regime had built for its own glorification. He was welcomed home with a ticker-tape parade through New York but had to ride a freight elevator at his own Waldorf-Astoria reception because Black guests were not permitted in the main elevators.
events.revealBlurb: August 3-9, 1936 — Jesse Owens. The story that Hitler refused to shake his hand is disputed; Hitler had stopped shaking any medal winners' hands after the first day. President Roosevelt never congratulated Owens; Owens said later: "Hitler didn't snub me — it was our president who snubbed me."

events.title: Bannister's 4-Minute Mile
events.blurb: A 25-year-old medical student in his final year of training, racing on a windy Oxford track in a university-versus-amateur competition, ran a mile in 3 minutes and 59.4 seconds — the first human ever to break the four-minute barrier. The record stood for 46 days. His pacers, who trailed off at the halfway and three-quarter marks on a pre-arranged plan, were athletes the newspapers had not noticed. Sport doctors had warned a sub-four mile might be physiologically impossible.
events.revealBlurb: May 6, 1954 — Roger Bannister at Iffley Road track. Pacers: Chris Brasher and Chris Chataway. John Landy of Australia broke Bannister's record 46 days later. Bannister beat him in the "Mile of the Century" race at the Vancouver Commonwealth Games in August 1954 — both running sub-four.

events.title: Cubs Win World Series
events.blurb: The Chicago Cubs won their first World Series championship in 108 years, defeating the Cleveland Indians in a 10-inning seventh game interrupted by a rain delay. The Cubs' championship drought — dating back to 1908 — was the longest in American professional sports. Their 1945 loss had been attributed by fans to the "Curse of the Billy Goat," thrown at the owner of a neighbourhood tavern who had been asked to remove his pet goat from a World Series game.
events.revealBlurb: November 2-3, 2016 — Cubs 8, Indians 7 in 10 innings at Progressive Field, Cleveland. The game ended at 12:47 AM local time on November 3. Cubs manager Joe Maddon, third baseman Kris Bryant, and first baseman Anthony Rizzo led the championship team. Chicago celebrated with a victory parade of 5 million people.

events.title: Kobe Bryant Dies
events.blurb: A 41-year-old retired basketball star, his 13-year-old daughter, and seven other passengers died when their private helicopter crashed into a hillside in thick fog outside Los Angeles while en route to a youth basketball game. The retired player had won five NBA championships, two Olympic golds, and the nickname "Black Mamba" during a 20-year career entirely with the Los Angeles Lakers. The crash prompted an outpouring of mourning around the world.
events.revealBlurb: January 26, 2020 — Kobe and Gianna Bryant. National Transportation Safety Board findings attributed the crash to pilot error in poor visibility. His 2017 jersey-retirement ceremony at Staples Center saw both his numbers (8 and 24) raised to the rafters — the only player in franchise history with multiple retired numbers.

events.title: Columbus Reaches the Americas
events.blurb: A Genoese navigator captaining three small Spanish ships, after 33 days of open-Atlantic sailing from the Canary Islands with an increasingly mutinous crew, sighted land just after 2 AM — a low-lying island he promptly named after a Christian saviour. He was convinced, and would die still convinced, that he had reached the outer islands of Asia. The four voyages he made over the next twelve years reshaped two continents.
events.revealBlurb: October 12, 1492 — Christopher Columbus made landfall on Guanahani in the Bahamas. The lookout who first sighted land, Rodrigo de Triana, did not receive the promised reward — Columbus claimed he had seen a light the previous evening. The contact collapsed Indigenous populations via epidemic disease within decades.

events.title: Magellan's Fleet Departs
events.blurb: Five ships and 270 sailors departed from Sanlúcar de Barrameda under a Portuguese navigator flying a Spanish flag, carrying provisions for two years. Three years later, one battered ship and 18 survivors returned — the first vessels to circumnavigate the globe, though their commander had been killed in a Filipino skirmish partway through.

events.title: Copernicus's De Revolutionibus
events.blurb: A 70-year-old Polish mathematician and canon of a cathedral in Warmia died on the same day he was reportedly handed a freshly printed copy of the book he had been writing, revising, and withholding from publication for three decades. The book, On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, argued that the earth was a planet orbiting the sun, and that the apparent daily motion of the heavens was actually the earth's own rotation. It was placed on the Papal Index 73 years later.
events.revealBlurb: May 24, 1543 — Nicolaus Copernicus died. The book's printer, Andreas Osiander, had added an anonymous preface describing its heliocentrism as a mere mathematical convenience; Copernicus probably never saw that preface. Galileo, who openly defended heliocentrism, was tried for heresy in 1633.

events.title: Drake Completes Circumnavigation
events.blurb: An English privateer, captaining one of five ships that had set out three years earlier on a raiding expedition against Spanish New World colonies, returned to his home port with holds full of Spanish silver and the honour of being the first Englishman — and second captain ever — to circumnavigate the globe. His queen personally knighted him on the deck of his ship. Spain's ambassador demanded his execution; the queen politely declined.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 1580 — Sir Francis Drake aboard the Golden Hind at Plymouth. Only his ship of the original five returned, with 59 of the original 164 men. The queen's share of the plunder more than doubled her annual government revenue for that year.

events.title: Spanish Armada Defeated
events.blurb: A Spanish naval force of 130 ships and 26,000 men, intended to escort a Flemish invasion army across the Channel to England, was met by a faster, more maneuverable English fleet off the Flanders coast. An English fireship attack scattered the Spanish anchorage overnight; the following day's running battle crippled the armada. Storms in the North Sea and along the Irish coast destroyed the rest on the long retreat home. Barely half returned to Spain.
events.revealBlurb: July 29 to August 8, 1588 — Battle of Gravelines decided it. English commanders: Lord Howard of Effingham, Sir Francis Drake. Roughly 35 Spanish ships reached home; most of the rest were wrecked on the Irish coast, whose people dealt harshly with survivors.

events.title: Narmer Unifies Upper and Lower Egypt
events.blurb: A king of Upper Egypt consolidated control over the Nile Delta region, creating a unified state stretching from the first cataract to the Mediterranean coast. The event is documented on a 64-centimeter ceremonial slate palette discovered at Hierakonpolis, which depicts the king wearing both the white crown of the south and the red crown of the north — the first known instance of that dual iconography. The palette is considered the earliest historical document in Egyptian history.
events.revealBlurb: c. 3100 BCE — Egypt. Narmer is likely the same person as the legendary "Menes." Modern Egyptologists treat the unification as a gradual process rather than a single conquest, but the Narmer Palette marks the symbolic moment it was first declared complete.

events.title: Sennacherib Destroys Babylon
events.blurb: An Assyrian king who had campaigned against the most sacred city in Mesopotamia multiple times finally sacked it completely, pulling down its temples, flooding the site to erase its foundations, and removing the statue of its principal god — an act considered the most sacrilegious in the ancient Near East. He took an estimated 200,000 captives and described the destruction in his own inscriptions as something the gods had ordained. He was murdered by two of his own sons eight years later.
events.revealBlurb: c. 689 BCE — Babylon. Sennacherib of Assyria. The removal of the statue of Marduk was so shocking that Babylonian priests spent decades constructing mythological explanations for why the god had permitted it. His son Esarhaddon rebuilt Babylon and returned Marduk's statue within a generation.

events.title: Battle of Carchemish
events.blurb: A Babylonian crown prince crushed a combined Egyptian and Assyrian force at a fortified trading city on the Euphrates River, ending any Egyptian military presence in the Levant and extinguishing the last organized remnant of a once-dominant power. The battle's outcome determined which empire would control the entire Fertile Crescent for the following seven decades. No Egyptian records of the battle survive — all accounts come from Babylonian and Hebrew sources.
events.revealBlurb: May/June 605 BCE — Carchemish (modern Turkey/Syria border). The Babylonian commander was Nebuchadnezzar II, not yet king; his father Nabopolassar died while the battle was being fought. Nebuchadnezzar rushed back to Babylon to claim the throne before rivals could act.

events.title: Library of Alexandria Established
events.blurb: A Macedonian king's scholarly advisor was charged with assembling a universal library in the new capital city — a building intended to collect every text ever written, in every language. Ships arriving in the harbor were searched for scrolls, which were confiscated, copied, and returned. The institution was attached to a research center called the Mouseion where scholars in medicine, mathematics, astronomy, and literature received royal stipends to work full-time.
events.revealBlurb: c. 295 BCE — Alexandria, Egypt. Conceived by Ptolemy I; built under Ptolemy II. Demetrius of Phalerum, an Athenian philosopher, was the founding librarian. The library eventually held an estimated 400,000–700,000 scrolls. It did not burn in a single dramatic fire — it declined gradually over centuries.

events.title: Death of Cleopatra
events.blurb: The last active pharaoh of a civilization three thousand years old died in her palace in Alexandria after her naval forces were destroyed off the Greek coast and her partner had already fallen on his sword. She was the seventh ruler to bear that name and the first in her dynasty to bother learning the Egyptian language. Her death ended a kingdom founded by one of Alexander the Great's generals, and within weeks it became a Roman province.
events.revealBlurb: August 12, 30 BCE — Alexandria. The asp-bite story comes from Plutarch, writing 130 years later; modern historians favor a fast-acting poison. She spoke nine languages. Her kingdom, the Ptolemaic dynasty, had lasted 275 years.

events.title: Fall of Tobruk
events.blurb: A fortified port city that had withstood a nine-month siege the previous year fell to an armoured assault in a single day, yielding 33,000 prisoners — including an entire South African division — along with 2,000 vehicles, 5,000 tons of food, and enough fuel to sustain the attacking force's advance for weeks.
events.revealBlurb: June 21, 1942. Churchill learned of Tobruk's fall while meeting Roosevelt in Washington — handed a pink slip of paper mid-meeting. Roosevelt's immediate response: "What can we do to help?" He arranged 300 Sherman tanks and 100 self-propelled guns for immediate shipment. The news triggered a no-confidence vote against Churchill in the House of Commons.

events.title: Italy's Armistice Announcement
events.blurb: A radio broadcast by a head of government announced that his country had signed an armistice with the opposing alliance, pulling out of an axis it had helped found, leaving its former partner's forces — which had already occupied key positions across the country — to decide how to respond. German forces immediately disarmed Italian troops and occupied cities across the peninsula.
events.revealBlurb: September 8, 1943 — Marshal Badoglio's broadcast at 7:42 PM. The armistice had actually been signed on September 3 but was kept secret. German Operation Achse activated within hours, disarming and capturing roughly 650,000 Italian soldiers. Many were sent to German labour camps; some 50,000 died in captivity. The king and Badoglio fled Rome before dawn.

events.title: Battle of the Bulge
events.blurb: 250,000 troops and nearly 1,000 tanks punched through the thinnest part of an Allied front in a snow-covered forested highland, achieving complete surprise and driving a 90-kilometre bulge into the line — the largest land battle ever fought by the United States Army, and the last major offensive Germany would ever launch in the west.
events.revealBlurb: December 16, 1944 – January 25, 1945. German soldiers wore American uniforms and used captured jeeps to spread chaos behind the lines; dozens were caught and executed. When the surrounded garrison at Bastogne was asked to surrender, Brigadier General Anthony McAuliffe replied with a single word: "Nuts!" The Germans had to ask for a translation.

events.title: Atomic Bombing of Hiroshima
events.blurb: A single aircraft flying at high altitude released a single bomb over a mid-sized city at 8:15 in the morning, detonating it 600 metres above a distinctive T-shaped bridge with the force of 15,000 tons of TNT — flattening 13 square kilometres, killing between 70,000 and 80,000 people instantly, and ultimately causing 140,000 deaths by the end of the year.
events.revealBlurb: August 6, 1945 — B-29 Enola Gay, piloted by Colonel Paul Tibbets, dropped "Little Boy" over Hiroshima. The aiming point was the Aioi Bridge. The bomb missed by about 250 metres but it did not matter. Tibbets's mother's name was Enola Gay. The co-pilot, Robert Lewis, wrote in his journal: "My God, what have we done?"

events.title: Atomic Bombing of Nagasaki
events.blurb: A second atomic strike, delivered three days after the first, detonated with the force of 22,000 tons of TNT over a city's industrial valley — but cloud cover over the primary target had forced the bomber to divert to its secondary, sparing one city and condemning another, while a city 160 kilometres away had been removed from the target list weeks earlier at the personal request of the American Secretary of War.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 1945 — the B-29 Bockscar dropped "Fat Man" at 11:02 AM. Kokura, the original target, was obscured by clouds; pilot Sweeney diverted to Nagasaki. An estimated 40,000 died instantly; 80,000 total by year's end. Secretary of War Stimson had personally removed Kyoto from the target list because he had visited it on his honeymoon and loved it.

events.title: Parthenon Marbles Completed
events.blurb: Under the direction of a single master sculptor, a team of Athenian craftsmen completed the exterior sculptural programme of a temple on a fortified limestone hill above their city — a continuous carved frieze 160 metres long depicting a civic religious procession, plus 92 metopes and two pediments. The sculptures were painted in vivid colours; the bleached white appearance known to modern viewers is an accident of weathering.
events.revealBlurb: c. 438 BCE — Phidias, chief sculptor of the Parthenon in Athens. Lord Elgin removed about half the surviving marbles between 1801 and 1812 and sold them to the British Museum. Greece has been asking for them back for over 200 years.

events.title: Giotto's Arena Chapel Frescoes
events.blurb: A Florentine painter completed a fresco cycle covering the interior walls of a small private chapel in a northern Italian city, commissioned by a banker trying to atone for his father's usury. The artist's naturalistic figures, three-dimensional space, and emotional humanism broke decisively with Byzantine conventions and set the visual vocabulary of the next three centuries. Vasari would later date the start of the Renaissance from his work.
events.revealBlurb: 1305 — Giotto di Bondone, at the Scrovegni (Arena) Chapel in Padua. Enrico Scrovegni built the chapel on the site of a Roman arena, and commissioned the frescoes to atone for the soul of his father, named in Dante's Inferno.

events.title: Raphael's School of Athens
events.blurb: A 28-year-old Umbrian painter completed the second of four monumental frescoes on the walls of the pope's private library at the Vatican, gathering the giants of classical philosophy into a single imaginary architectural space. Plato and Aristotle walk forward from a vanishing point; Pythagoras writes in a book, Euclid draws on a slate, Heraclitus leans alone on a block. The face of Euclid is the architect Bramante; Heraclitus is Michelangelo, working bitterly next door.
events.revealBlurb: 1511 — Raphael Sanzio, in the Stanza della Segnatura. The rivalry with Michelangelo, then painting the Sistine Ceiling a short walk away, was real; Raphael added him as an afterthought in a late revision.

events.title: Sistine Chapel Ceiling Unveiled
events.blurb: A 37-year-old Florentine sculptor, who had accepted a papal commission reluctantly after four years insisting he was not a painter, unveiled 500 square metres of freshly painted fresco covering the ceiling of a Vatican chapel. The work, which had taken four years, depicted nine scenes from Genesis surrounded by 300 figures. The artist had painted it while standing, not lying down as myth claims, his neck bent back for hours daily.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1512 — Michelangelo Buonarroti. He wrote a sonnet complaining of his neck: "I've grown a goiter by dwelling in this den… my beard turns up to heaven." Restoration between 1980 and 1994 revealed vivid colours under 400 years of candle smoke.

events.title: Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring
events.blurb: A Dutch painter in his early thirties completed an intimate oil study on canvas of a young woman turning toward the viewer, her head covered in a blue and yellow turban, a single teardrop-shaped pearl catching the light at her ear. It was not a commissioned portrait but a "tronie" — a character study. The artist made only about 35 paintings in his career; this one was rediscovered in 1881 at auction for two guilders.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1665 — Johannes Vermeer. Now in the Mauritshuis in The Hague. The "pearl" may actually be tin or glass — no pearl of that size is plausible. Tracy Chevalier's 1999 novel and the 2003 film made it a pop-culture icon.

events.title: Dred Scott Decision
events.blurb: The Supreme Court ruled 7–2 that Dred Scott, an enslaved man who had lived in free states and territories, had no right to sue for his freedom — and that Congress had never possessed the authority to ban slavery from the territories, thereby invalidating the Missouri Compromise. Chief Justice Roger Taney further held that Black Americans, free or enslaved, were not citizens and had "no rights which the white man was bound to respect."
events.revealBlurb: March 6, 1857 — Washington, D.C. The ruling was intended to settle the slavery question definitively; instead it inflamed the North and energized the new Republican Party. Dred Scott was freed by his original owner's family two months after the decision. He died 16 months later, a free man.

events.title: Atomic Bomb Dropped on Hiroshima
events.blurb: At 8:15 that morning, a B-29 Superfortress named the Enola Gay released a uranium bomb nicknamed "Little Boy" over the Japanese city of Hiroshima, which detonated at 1,968 feet above the city center with a force equivalent to approximately 15,000 tons of TNT. Estimates of deaths in the four months following the explosion range from 90,000 to 166,000; roughly two-thirds of the city's buildings were destroyed.
events.revealBlurb: August 6, 1945 — Hiroshima, Japan. "Little Boy" was the first nuclear weapon ever used in warfare, but it had never been fully tested — scientists were confident enough in the gun-type design. Japan did not surrender after Hiroshima; it took a second bomb (Nagasaki, August 9) to produce the surrender announcement.

events.title: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg Executed
events.blurb: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were executed by electric chair at Sing Sing Prison, having been convicted of passing atomic bomb design secrets to the Soviet Union — making them the only American civilians executed for espionage during the Cold War. Their case divided the nation, with their guilt debated in editorial pages, union halls, and diplomatic cables around the world.
events.revealBlurb: June 19, 1953 — Ossining, New York. Ethel Rosenberg required three jolts of electricity before she died; Julius was pronounced dead after the first. Subsequent release of Soviet archives confirmed Julius was a spy; historians still debate the extent of Ethel's involvement.

events.title: Nixon Resigns the Presidency
events.blurb: That evening, Richard Nixon became the first and only U.S. president to resign from office, delivering a nationally televised address from the Oval Office in which he announced his departure would take effect at noon the following day. The resignation came after the release of the "smoking gun" tape proved Nixon had personally directed the Watergate cover-up six days after the break-in, making his impeachment and Senate conviction certain.
events.revealBlurb: August 8, 1974 — The Oval Office. Nixon's approval rating the week of his resignation was 24%. Gerald Ford pardoned him one month later, saying "our long national nightmare is over" — a pardon that likely cost Ford the 1976 election. Nixon is the only president ever to resign.

events.title: House Impeaches President Clinton
events.blurb: The House of Representatives voted to impeach President Bill Clinton on the 19th of that month, on charges of perjury before a grand jury (228–206) and obstruction of justice (221–212) arising from his false testimony about a sexual relationship with White House intern Monica Lewinsky. Clinton became only the second U.S. president ever to be impeached; the Senate acquitted him on both articles the following February.
events.revealBlurb: December 19, 1998 — U.S. Capitol. The vote occurred while U.S. warplanes were bombing Iraq (Operation Desert Fox), which the White House denied was timed to distract from the impeachment. House Speaker-designate Bob Livingston resigned that same day. Clinton's approval rating on the day of his impeachment was 73%.

events.title: Pont du Gard Built
events.blurb: A three-tiered limestone aqueduct bridge was constructed to carry water 50 kilometres across southern Gaul to the Roman colony of Nemausus (modern Nîmes). The top level — 48 metres above the River Gard — still carried its channel; the whole structure spans 275 metres. It was built dry, without mortar, using stones so precisely cut that the joints remain watertight after two millennia. The aqueduct itself was decommissioned in the 6th century; the bridge survived as a road crossing.
events.revealBlurb: c. 50 CE — built under Emperor Claudius. The water it carried had a gradient of only 1 in 3,000 — about 30 centimetres of drop per kilometre. The Pont du Gard is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most visited tourist destinations in France.

events.title: Hagia Sophia Consecrated
events.blurb: A vast domed cathedral, built in a Bosphorus imperial capital in just five years by 10,000 labourers, was consecrated with a grand procession. Its 31-metre-diameter dome seemed to float on light — a feat of engineering that would not be surpassed in Europe for nearly a thousand years. The emperor who commissioned it allegedly exclaimed: "Solomon, I have surpassed thee!"
events.revealBlurb: December 27, 537 — Constantinople (now Istanbul), under Justinian I. Architects were Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, both mathematicians. Converted to a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1934, and a mosque again in 2020.

events.title: Leaning Tower of Pisa Begun
events.blurb: Construction began on a free-standing bell tower for the cathedral complex of an Italian city-state on the Tuscan coast. By the time three of its eight stories were finished five years later, the soft alluvial ground beneath the south side was already sinking noticeably. Construction was halted for nearly a century. When work resumed, builders attempted to compensate by building upper floors taller on the low side — so the tower is actually curved. It was completed 199 years after ground-breaking.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 1173 — Pisa Cathedral bell tower. The tilt is currently about 3.97 degrees after stabilization work completed in 2008. Galileo is said to have dropped balls of different weights from it to demonstrate they fall at the same rate — the story is almost certainly apocryphal.

events.title: Panama Canal Opens
events.blurb: A 77-kilometre canal cutting across the narrowest part of the Central American isthmus opened to international shipping, after a US-run construction effort that had finished a French attempt abandoned two decades earlier amid malaria, yellow fever, and bankruptcy. The canal used a system of locks to raise ships 26 metres above sea level across the continental divide. It cut the sea route from New York to San Francisco by over 12,000 kilometres.
events.revealBlurb: August 15, 1914 — the ship SS Ancon made the first full transit. The American construction was made possible partly by controlling yellow fever and malaria through mosquito eradication. The 1977 Torrijos-Carter treaties returned the canal to Panamanian sovereignty in 1999.

events.title: Golden Gate Bridge Opens
events.blurb: A 2,737-metre suspension bridge painted international orange opened across a strait connecting San Francisco Bay to the Pacific Ocean. At the time the longest suspension span in the world (1,280 metres between its towers), it had been built through the Depression with labour recruited off bread lines and union halls. Workers wore (then-innovative) hard hats and safety harnesses; a net slung below the deck saved 19 men who fell, dubbed the "Halfway to Hell Club."
events.revealBlurb: May 27, 1937 — engineer Joseph Strauss, architect Irving Morrow. 200,000 people walked across on opening day. The famous "international orange" color is maintained by a full-time crew of 38 painters. Bridge suicides have been an anguishing running tally; a suicide barrier was finally completed in 2024.

events.title: Charlemagne Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A Frankish king, in a papal basilica in the old western imperial capital for Christmas Mass, rose from prayer to be unexpectedly crowned "Emperor of the Romans" by the pope. The coronation resurrected, at least in title, a western empire that had been extinct for 324 years, and established a relationship between popes and emperors that would shape European politics for eight centuries.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 800 — Charlemagne in Rome, crowned by Pope Leo III. Charlemagne later claimed he had been surprised — but the pope probably wouldn't have dared without his consent. The Holy Roman Empire survived in one form or another until 1806.

events.title: Treaty of Verdun
events.blurb: Three grandsons of Charlemagne, after a three-year civil war, signed a treaty in a French town dividing their grandfather's empire into three kingdoms — a western Frankish one destined to become France, an eastern one destined to become Germany, and a middle strip whose ownership would be disputed for a thousand years.
events.revealBlurb: August 843 — Louis the German got the east, Charles the Bald got the west, Lothair got the middle (Lotharingia, surviving in "Lorraine"). The France–Germany border problem is essentially a 1,200-year-old inheritance dispute.

events.title: William the Conqueror Crowned
events.blurb: Ten weeks after winning a decisive battle on the south coast of England, the Norman duke who had invaded was crowned king at a Westminster abbey. During the coronation, Norman guards outside the abbey mistook acclamations for riot and set fire to nearby houses; the new king was hurriedly anointed while smoke drifted through the doors. He would never be popular with his new subjects.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 1066 — Westminster Abbey. William spent the next two decades building castles, compiling the Domesday Book, and crushing rebellions. He was buried in Caen, and his tomb was opened, profaned, and emptied of bones during the French Revolution.

events.title: Saladin Retakes Jerusalem
events.blurb: A Kurdish Muslim sultan, having crushed a Crusader field army three months earlier at the Horns of Hattin, accepted the peaceful surrender of the holy city from its desperate defenders after an eight-day siege. In contrast to the bloody Frankish sack of the city 88 years earlier, he permitted ransomed Christians to leave with their possessions and freed many who could not pay. News of the fall triggered the Third Crusade.
events.revealBlurb: October 2, 1187 — Saladin. His reputation for chivalry, magnified by his later adversary Richard the Lionheart, made him a hero of medieval European literature despite being its opponent. Dante placed him in Limbo rather than Hell.

events.title: Genghis Khan Unites the Mongols
events.blurb: A 44-year-old tribal chieftain named Temüjin, having spent two decades defeating his rivals across the eastern steppe, was acclaimed "Universal Ruler" at an assembly of chieftains beside a sacred river. Within two decades his cavalry armies would sack Beijing, overrun Persia, and reach the Adriatic, creating the largest contiguous land empire in history.
events.revealBlurb: 1206 — at the Onon River. The title "Genghis Khan" is a western rendering; contemporary Mongol sources call him Činggis Qa'an. Genetic studies suggest roughly 16 million men alive today descend from his Y-chromosome line.

events.title: Sargon Founds the Akkadian Empire
events.blurb: A royal cupbearer of Mesopotamian origin, whose own infancy legends described a reed-basket journey down a river, overthrew his king and went on to subdue the patchwork of Sumerian city-states that had squabbled for centuries. He united them under a single administration that stretched from the Mediterranean coast to the Persian Gulf, establishing what is generally considered the first empire in human history.
events.revealBlurb: c. 2334 BCE — Sargon of Akkad. His dynasty lasted roughly 180 years before collapsing under external pressure. His granddaughter Enheduanna, high priestess at Ur, became the first named author in world literature. The famous "Mask of Sargon" bronze portrait is either him or a successor — ambiguous.

events.title: Battle of Thermopylae
events.blurb: A force of 300 Spartan hoplites with their personal attendants, reinforced by perhaps 7,000 other Greek allies, held a narrow coastal pass for three days against a vastly larger Persian army. On the third day, betrayed by a local goatherd who revealed a mountain path, the Persians flanked the defenders. The Spartan king dismissed most of his allies and stayed with his three hundred to die. The sacrifice bought time for the evacuation of Athens and the Greek fleet's preparation.
events.revealBlurb: August 480 BCE — King Leonidas of Sparta vs. Xerxes I. Persian force size is debated; Herodotus' claim of millions is obviously inflated. Modern estimates suggest 70,000 to 300,000. "Molon labe" — "come and take them" — is Leonidas' reported reply to a demand that the Greeks surrender their arms.

events.title: Alexander the Great Dies
events.blurb: A 32-year-old conqueror, having created an empire stretching from Macedonia to northwestern India in ten years of campaigning, died of fever (or poisoning — sources disagree) in a palace in a Mesopotamian capital while planning the next campaign, this one against Arabia. He left no clear heir; his generals divided the empire into warring successor states — the Hellenistic kingdoms — that shaped Mediterranean culture for the next three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: June 10 or 11, 323 BCE — Alexander III in Babylon. Asked on his deathbed to whom his empire should go, he reportedly said: "To the strongest." Competing theories for his death: malaria, typhoid, alcoholism, West Nile virus, poisoning by his general Antipater. His body was hijacked en route home by Ptolemy to Alexandria.

events.title: The Antonine Plague
events.blurb: Soldiers returning from campaigns in Parthia brought a disease — almost certainly smallpox — that spread from the eastern frontier through every province of the empire over fifteen years. The physician Galen, the most famous doctor of his age, documented symptoms in detail from Rome itself; at the plague's peak witnesses recorded 2,000 deaths per day in the capital alone.
events.revealBlurb: 165–180 CE. Galen's treatment recommendation included keeping patients warm and feeding them milk — the best care available, and completely ineffective. The plague killed co-emperor Lucius Verus in 169 CE and may have killed up to 10% of the empire's total population.

events.title: Battle of Adrianople
events.blurb: After Rome settled Visigothic refugees south of the Danube and then systematically starved and abused them, the Goths rose in revolt. Emperor Valens — who refused to wait for reinforcements — attacked their fortified camp with approximately 30,000 men. Gothic cavalry flanked both sides of the Roman line and trapped the legions; two-thirds of the eastern field army was destroyed and Valens himself was killed.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 378 CE. Valens's body was never found. One account says he was carried wounded to a farmhouse, which Gothic soldiers then set alight; another says he was lost in the general slaughter. Military historians sometimes call Adrianople "the ancient world's Stalingrad."

events.title: Intel 4004 Released
events.blurb: A Silicon Valley chipmaker released the first commercial microprocessor — a single integrated circuit 3 millimetres long containing 2,300 transistors, clocking at 740 kilohertz, capable of computing roughly as fast as the 30-tonne ENIAC 25 years earlier. It had been developed as a calculator chip for a Japanese customer. Its designers convinced Intel's management to retain the design rights and market it as a general-purpose product.
events.revealBlurb: November 15, 1971 — Intel 4004. Designers Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, Stanley Mazor, and Masatoshi Shima. The 4-bit chip cost $200. Intel's 1971 product-line predecessor was the 3101 memory chip; it now sells trillions of transistors per year.

events.title: IBM Personal Computer Launched
events.blurb: A technology corporation released a personal computer based on an Intel processor running an operating system licensed from a small software company for $25,000. Its open architecture allowed third-party manufacturers to build compatible clones, spawning a global personal computer industry worth trillions within a decade.

events.title: IBM PC Released
events.blurb: The world's dominant mainframe computer maker released a small desktop machine built, unusually for the company, from off-the-shelf parts — an Intel 8088 processor, an operating system licensed from Microsoft, components any competitor could buy. Business customers trusted the name and bought millions. The design's open specifications led to a decade of "IBM compatible" clones that collectively made the Intel/Microsoft duopoly inevitable.
events.revealBlurb: August 12, 1981 — IBM PC model 5150. It had 16KB of RAM and no hard drive. IBM's decision to source DOS from Microsoft, rather than write it in-house, is usually cited as the great strategic error of 20th-century computing. Gates retained all distribution rights.

events.title: iPhone Announced
events.blurb: A California computer company's co-founder unveiled a new class of mobile phone at a San Francisco conference, combining a widescreen iPod, a mobile internet browser, and a phone into a single slim device controlled entirely by a multi-touch finger-driven screen. He dialled a coffee shop on stage to demonstrate. Nokia's executives watching the announcement reportedly laughed at its lack of a physical keyboard; BlackBerry's CEO later admitted they also underestimated it.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 2007 — Steve Jobs at Macworld. It went on sale June 29. The original did not support 3G, had no copy-and-paste, and shipped without an App Store — those all came in subsequent years. Apple now makes over $200 billion a year just from iPhones.

events.title: AlphaGo Beats Lee Sedol
events.blurb: A London-based artificial intelligence laboratory's go-playing program, trained on millions of human games and then on games it had played against itself, defeated the reigning world champion of the ancient Asian board game 4–1 in a five-game match in Seoul. The match was broadcast live to 280 million people. Experts had predicted a champion-beating go program was a decade away; the algorithmic gap between games like chess and go had seemed insurmountable.
events.revealBlurb: March 15, 2016 — DeepMind's AlphaGo vs. Lee Sedol. Lee's single winning game, move 78 — the "divine move" — exploited a subtle blind spot in the AI. DeepMind was acquired by Google in 2014 for around $500 million. Lee retired from professional go three years later, partly because AI had changed the game.

events.title: Berlin Wall Construction Begins
events.blurb: East German soldiers and workers erected barbed-wire barricades along the full length of the border between East and West Berlin overnight, sealing the most visible escape route from the Eastern Bloc without advance public announcement. Within days, temporary barriers were replaced with concrete, dividing families who had crossed freely just the day before.

events.title: Cuban Missile Crisis Address
events.blurb: An American president delivered a 17-minute televised address revealing that Soviet nuclear missiles had been discovered on a Caribbean island 145 kilometres from Florida, demanding their removal within a strict deadline. The 13-day standoff that followed was the closest the Cold War came to nuclear exchange, with submarines on both sides carrying armed torpedoes.

events.title: Prague Spring Invasion
events.blurb: Reform-minded leaders in a central European capital had spent eight months experimenting with "socialism with a human face" — easing censorship, rehabilitating purge victims, and tolerating debate. In the night, 250,000 Warsaw Pact soldiers and 2,000 tanks rolled across the borders. Unarmed civilians tried to argue with the invading soldiers; within days the reforms were reversed.
events.revealBlurb: August 20-21, 1968 — invasion of Czechoslovakia. Reformist leader Alexander Dubček was flown to Moscow and forced to sign a capitulation. A student named Jan Palach set himself on fire in Wenceslas Square five months later in protest.

events.title: SDI Announced
events.blurb: In a televised address from the Oval Office, a U.S. president proposed a space-based missile defense shield intended to render nuclear weapons "impotent and obsolete." Critics dubbed it "Star Wars" and scientists called it technically unachievable. Whatever its technical merits, the announcement terrified the Kremlin and forced Soviet planners to contemplate a ruinous new arms race they could not afford.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 1983 — Reagan's Strategic Defense Initiative. It never produced a working system, but it contributed to Soviet economic exhaustion. Some historians credit SDI with accelerating Gorbachev's arms-control pivot by years.

events.title: KAL 007 Shot Down
events.blurb: A Korean civilian airliner carrying 269 passengers and crew strayed over Soviet airspace over the Sea of Japan on a flight from New York to Seoul. A Sukhoi interceptor fired two air-to-air missiles and the 747 broke apart over international waters. The Kremlin at first denied any involvement; the United States released taped radio transmissions of the shootdown within a week.
events.revealBlurb: September 1, 1983 — a U.S. congressman, Larry McDonald, was among the dead. Reagan called it an "act of barbarism." The incident led directly to the U.S. decision to make GPS available for civilian use, so no passenger aircraft would ever again stray for lack of navigation.

events.title: 19th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: Seven decades after a convention in upstate New York had narrowly resolved that women ought to vote, a Tennessee state legislator cast the deciding vote for his state's ratification — after reading a telegram from his mother urging him to do so. Women across the United States gained the national vote in time for the November presidential election, in which 8 million new voters participated.
events.revealBlurb: August 18, 1920 — the deciding vote was cast by Harry T. Burn, age 24. His mother's letter read: "Hurrah, and vote for suffrage. Don't keep them in doubt." The amendment was certified on August 26, now Women's Equality Day.

events.title: Universal Declaration of Human Rights
events.blurb: The United Nations General Assembly, meeting in a Paris exhibition hall, adopted a declaration of 30 articles enumerating rights that every human being was to be considered entitled to by virtue of humanity itself. The document's drafting committee, chaired by the widow of a U.S. president, had spent two years negotiating across ideological and cultural lines. No state voted against; eight abstained.
events.revealBlurb: December 10, 1948 — Eleanor Roosevelt chaired the drafting committee. Adopted 48-0 with 8 abstentions (Soviet bloc, Saudi Arabia, South Africa). Translated into over 500 languages — more than any other document. December 10 is now International Human Rights Day.

events.title: FDA Approves the Pill
events.blurb: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved a daily oral contraceptive pill combining synthetic estrogen and progestin for sale as a birth-control product, two years after approving the same drug for menstrual disorders. Over two million American women were taking it within three years. It was the first drug ever developed for use by healthy people rather than sick ones, and it reshaped women's labour-force participation for the next half-century.
events.revealBlurb: May 9, 1960 — Enovid, made by G.D. Searle. The research had been funded privately by heiress Katharine McCormick because federal funding was politically impossible. Single women could be denied prescriptions until a 1972 Supreme Court ruling.

events.title: Margaret Thatcher Becomes PM
events.blurb: The leader of the British Conservative Party, a grocer's daughter who had studied chemistry at Oxford and later trained as a barrister, was invited by the monarch to form a government after her party won a sweeping parliamentary majority. She became the United Kingdom's first woman prime minister and would hold the office for 11 years — the longest continuous premiership of the 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1979 — she took office quoting St. Francis of Assisi on the doorstep: "Where there is discord, may we bring harmony." The next decade would be anything but that. She was forced to resign by her own cabinet in November 1990.

events.title: Ruth Bader Ginsburg Confirmed
events.blurb: A 60-year-old federal appeals court judge, a former ACLU lawyer who had successfully argued six of the era's most important gender-discrimination cases before the court she was now joining, was confirmed 96-3 as the second woman to sit on the U.S. Supreme Court. She would serve 27 years, becoming — somewhat unexpectedly for a cautious litigator — a late-life pop-culture icon on the Court's liberal wing.
events.revealBlurb: August 10, 1993 — nominated by Bill Clinton. She acquired the nickname "Notorious RBG" from a law student's Tumblr in 2013. She died September 18, 2020, enabling the confirmation of Amy Coney Barrett eight days before the presidential election.

events.title: Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake Premieres
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Russian composer's first full-length ballet score premiered at a grand theatre in the Russian capital, paired with choreography that was widely thought incompetent and dancing that was widely thought under-rehearsed. Critics focused their complaints on the music, which they found too "symphonic" for dancing. Only after the composer's death, in a restaged 1895 version with new choreography, did the ballet become a classic.
events.revealBlurb: March 4, 1877 — Pyotr Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake at the Bolshoi, Moscow (Old Style February 20). The 1895 St. Petersburg revival with Petipa/Ivanov choreography is the version most companies perform today. The tragic black-swan finale was a 1950s restoration.

events.title: The Rite of Spring Riot
events.blurb: A 30-year-old Russian composer's ballet score, depicting a pagan spring ritual with jagged rhythms, dissonant chord stacks, and primitivist choreography, premiered at a new Paris theatre and nearly caused a full-scale audience riot. Shouts, whistles, and fistfights broke out within minutes; the choreographer had to shout counts to dancers from the wings because they couldn't hear the orchestra. The piece is now considered one of the pivotal works of 20th-century music.
events.revealBlurb: May 29, 1913 — Igor Stravinsky and Ballets Russes at Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, Paris. Choreography by Vaslav Nijinsky. The Parisian critic Carl Van Vechten reported his seat-neighbour beating rhythmically on his head with his fists in distress.

events.title: Woodstock Festival Opens
events.blurb: A music festival on a dairy farm in upstate New York that had sold 186,000 advance tickets was overwhelmed by more than 400,000 attendees in the preceding 48 hours, forcing organisers to declare it a free event and abandon the ticket booths. Thirty-two acts performed over four rain-soaked days, and the festival became the defining cultural gathering of its generation.

events.title: Woodstock Festival
events.blurb: A three-day music festival, overcapacity within hours of opening, drew an estimated 400,000 young people to a dairy farm in upstate New York despite severe rain. Fences collapsed; the event became de facto free. 32 acts performed — Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, The Who, Santana, Creedence Clearwater Revival, Joan Baez. Two people died (one from an overdose, one crushed by a tractor); two babies were born. The festival became the defining symbol of the 1960s counterculture.
events.revealBlurb: August 15-18, 1969 — on Max Yasgur's farm in Bethel, NY. Hendrix closed at 9 AM Monday morning to a dwindling crowd with a distorted, feedback-laced "Star-Spangled Banner." The 1970 documentary won an Oscar.

events.title: Led Zeppelin IV Released
events.blurb: A British rock band released their fourth album with no title, no text, and no band name anywhere on the cover — just a painting of an old man with a bundle of firewood on his back. The album contained eight tracks, including an eight-minute multi-part track that would become the most-played song on American FM radio for a decade. Critics were lukewarm; listeners bought 37 million copies.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1971 — Led Zeppelin IV, featuring "Stairway to Heaven." The band was so angered by critical reception of the previous album that they refused to identify themselves on this one. The old man on the cover was a real picture bought from an antique shop in Reading.

events.title: Wagner's Ring Cycle Premieres
events.blurb: A 63-year-old German composer presented the first complete four-night performance of a 15-hour operatic cycle he had been writing, off and on, for 26 years, at a festival opera house in a Bavarian town he had specifically had built to host it. Audiences included Tchaikovsky, Liszt, Grieg, Bruckner, the emperor of Germany, and the emperor of Brazil. The complete run was a financial disaster.
events.revealBlurb: August 13-17, 1876 — Richard Wagner at the Bayreuth Festspielhaus, Bayreuth. The festival runs to this day; tickets are difficult to obtain. Wagner's anti-Semitic essays, and the Nazi regime's later embrace of his work, have cast a lasting shadow.

events.title: First Jazz Recording
events.blurb: Five white musicians from New Orleans, working under the slightly misspelled name "Original Dixieland Jass Band," recorded two sides for a Victor label at a New York studio: "Livery Stable Blues" and "Dixie Jass Band One Step." The 78 sold a million copies, breaking sales records, and introduced the word "jazz" to most Americans. Black New Orleans musicians had been playing the style for years; the first commercial recording went to imitators.
events.revealBlurb: February 26, 1917 — recorded in NYC; released March 7, 1917. The ODJB's cornetist Nick LaRocca later claimed, implausibly, to have invented jazz. The ethical irony of white performers first commercializing a Black art form was noted at the time and has only grown.

events.title: Elvis Presley Dies
events.blurb: A 42-year-old singer was found unresponsive on a bathroom floor of his Memphis mansion in the early afternoon and pronounced dead at a local hospital an hour later. The cause was heart failure, probably exacerbated by a cocktail of barbiturates prescribed by his personal physician. 80,000 mourners lined the four-kilometre route to the cemetery; his face had appeared on 150 magazine covers in his lifetime and would appear on tens of thousands more after his death.
events.revealBlurb: August 16, 1977 — Elvis Presley at Graceland, Memphis. An autopsy found 14 different drugs in his system. His doctor, George Nichopoulos, had his license revoked years later. "Elvis sightings" began the day after the funeral and have never entirely stopped.

events.title: Live Aid
events.blurb: Two simultaneous 16-hour benefit concerts, one at a stadium in London and one at a stadium in Philadelphia, were broadcast live to an estimated 1.9 billion people in 150 countries — at the time perhaps 40 percent of the world population. The concerts raised around $127 million for Ethiopian famine relief. A British band's 21-minute set, by most accounts, stole the whole day. Its lead singer's synchronized clap-along with 72,000 people is the stuff of legend.
events.revealBlurb: July 13, 1985 — Wembley Stadium and JFK Stadium. The stealing-the-show band was Queen, Freddie Mercury at Wembley. Co-organizers Bob Geldof and Midge Ure. "Feed the World" had been launched by the Band Aid charity single the previous Christmas.

events.title: Spotify Launches
events.blurb: A Swedish music-streaming service, developed in Stockholm and Stockholm alone for two years, launched invitation-only to users in six European countries. The service offered an enormous music library — eventually over 100 million tracks — free with ads or $10/month without. It would restructure the entire music business: album sales collapsed, streaming became the default, and royalties flowed through aggregation models that artists found miserly.
events.revealBlurb: October 7, 2008 — founded by Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon. The service arrived in the U.S. in July 2011 after lengthy negotiations with major labels. It had 620 million monthly active users as of 2024 — the largest audio subscription service ever.

events.title: Watt's Separate Condenser Patent
events.blurb: A Scottish instrument maker received a patent for a steam engine design that used a separate condenser chamber, dramatically reducing fuel consumption. Unlike earlier designs that wasted energy reheating the main cylinder on every stroke, the new engine converted roughly 75% more heat into mechanical work.

events.title: Fulton's Clermont Steamboat
events.blurb: A 41-year-old American engineer piloted a 40-metre paddlewheel steamboat he had built with financing from a New York politician 240 kilometres up the Hudson River from New York City to Albany, against the current, in 32 hours — a trip that had previously taken sailing sloops four days. The voyage proved steam-powered river transport commercially viable, revolutionizing inland commerce across the newly expanded United States.
events.revealBlurb: August 17, 1807 — Robert Fulton's Clermont. Spectators along the riverbanks initially took the steam-belching boat for a dragon. Fulton held a 30-year steamboat monopoly on New York waters, broken by the 1824 Supreme Court case Gibbons v. Ogden, which is still taught in law schools.

events.title: Peterloo Massacre
events.blurb: A crowd of perhaps 60,000 people had gathered on a large open field in a northern English mill city to hear speakers demand parliamentary reform. Local magistrates ordered mounted cavalry to arrest the lead speaker and charge into the crowd. Eighteen people were killed — including a two-year-old child — and hundreds injured. The incident, sardonically named after the Battle of Waterloo four years earlier, became a rallying point for British reform movements for decades.
events.revealBlurb: August 16, 1819 — St Peter's Field, Manchester. The press-blackened newspaper of the day printed the event in black-bordered pages. Shelley wrote "The Mask of Anarchy" in response; it was not published until 1832 out of fear of prosecution. The Peterloo Memorial in Manchester was unveiled in 2019.

events.title: Bell Patents Telephone
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Scottish-born American inventor was granted a patent on "the method of, and apparatus for, transmitting vocal or other sounds telegraphically." Three days later he made the first recognized telephone call in his Boston laboratory, summoning his assistant from the next room. The patent, filed the same morning as a rival inventor's competing application, would become the most valuable patent ever issued by the US government.
events.revealBlurb: March 7, 1876 — Alexander Graham Bell. The first call: "Mr. Watson — come here — I want to see you." The rival, Elisha Gray, filed his caveat a few hours later; legal battles continued for years. American Telephone & Telegraph, founded on Bell's patent, became the largest corporation in the world.

events.title: Wright Brothers' First Flight
events.blurb: Two American bicycle-shop owners from Dayton, Ohio achieved the first sustained, controlled, powered flight of a heavier-than-air aircraft on a windswept dune at the Outer Banks of North Carolina. The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 36 metres — about the wingspan of a modern commercial airliner. They made three more flights that morning; the fourth covered 260 metres in 59 seconds. Few newspapers reported the achievement; commercial aviation took another three decades to arrive.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1903 — Orville and Wilbur Wright at Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, NC. The flyer is now in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum. The pair spent 4 years after their first flight battling patent disputes and litigation rather than manufacturing planes.

events.title: Galileo Observes the Moon Through a Telescope
events.blurb: Turning a new optical instrument toward the night sky, an Italian mathematician observed that the Moon's surface was rough, mountainous, and marked by craters — directly contradicting the ancient belief that celestial bodies were perfect smooth spheres. Careful drawings of the shadow lines allowed him to estimate the height of lunar mountains by triangulating shadow lengths.
events.revealBlurb: November 30, 1609 — Galileo had only heard a description of a Dutch spyglass and built his own without ever seeing one. His 1610 pamphlet Sidereus Nuncius went through its entire print run within a week. He dedicated Jupiter's four moons to the Medici family to secure patronage — an early example of branded science.

events.title: Electromagnetic Field Equations Published
events.blurb: A Scottish physicist unified electricity, magnetism, and light into a single mathematical framework of four equations, showing that changing electric fields produce magnetic fields and vice versa — generating self-propagating waves that travel at the speed of light. The equations predicted that light was an electromagnetic wave and implied the existence of radio waves, infrared radiation, and other forms not yet observed.
events.revealBlurb: 1865 — James Clerk Maxwell's paper was read to the Royal Society in December 1864. Heinrich Hertz experimentally confirmed the existence of radio waves in 1887, nine years after Maxwell died of cancer at 48. Richard Feynman called Maxwell's equations "the most significant event of the 19th century" — a bold statement given the century's competition.

events.title: Helium Detected in the Sun
events.blurb: During a total solar eclipse, a French astronomer studying the spectrum of light from the Sun's outer atmosphere found a bright yellow spectral line that matched no known element on Earth, suggesting the existence of a new element present in the Sun but not yet found on our planet. Two months later, an English astronomer independently identified the same line and gave the element its name, derived from the Greek word for the Sun.
events.revealBlurb: August 18, 1868 — Janssen realised during the eclipse that the bright chromospheric lines could be observed in daylight without an eclipse and invented the spectroscope for doing so. Helium was not detected on Earth for another 27 years, when it was found in a uranium mineral in 1895. It is the only element discovered in space before being found on Earth.

events.title: Special Relativity Paper Published
events.blurb: A 30-page paper demolished the concept of absolute time, arguing that the speed of light is the same for all observers regardless of their motion, and that simultaneity, length, and mass all depend on relative velocity. The paper contained no citations, because its author — a patent clerk working in his spare time — had arrived at the theory by pure thought experiment.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 1905 — one of four papers the same author submitted to Annalen der Physik that year, including one on Brownian motion and one that would later win the Nobel Prize for the photoelectric effect. The mass-energy equivalence paper (E=mc²) followed two months later.

events.title: Human Genome Project Completed
events.blurb: An international consortium announced the completion of a map of the entire 3-billion-letter chemical sequence of human DNA, covering 99 percent of gene-containing regions at 99.99 percent accuracy — two years ahead of schedule. The project, begun in 1990, required coordinating laboratories across six countries and produced a reference sequence that has underpinned virtually every major advance in genetic medicine since.
events.revealBlurb: April 14, 2003 — a rival private effort by Celera Genomics, led by Craig Venter, raced the public consortium and forced both teams to declare a joint "completion" in 2000. The actual finished sequence was only completed in 2003. A truly gapless human genome wasn't assembled until 2022, when long-read sequencing technology filled the remaining 8%.

events.title: Rashomon Released
events.blurb: A 40-year-old Japanese director released a 88-minute film in which the same violent encounter is recounted by four different participants, none of whom agrees with any of the others. The Venice Film Festival awarded it the Golden Lion the following year, and the world film industry discovered Japanese cinema as a major force. The very title became an English noun: "the Rashomon effect" is the concept of contradictory memories.
events.revealBlurb: August 26, 1950 — Akira Kurosawa. The producers were reportedly baffled by the script and wanted it re-edited. Its Venice win completely blindsided Japanese critics, who had not thought much of the film. It led directly to the global reception of Ozu, Mizoguchi, and Kurosawa's later work.

events.title: Tokyo Story Released
events.blurb: A Japanese director released a 136-minute film about an elderly provincial couple who travel to the capital to visit their adult children, only to find them too busy with their own lives. Its stationary low-angle camera, dialogues shot face-on toward the audience, and refusal of conventional emotional climax embodied the director's signature style. Polls of international critics and filmmakers regularly rank it among the greatest films ever made.
events.revealBlurb: November 3, 1953 — Yasujirō Ozu. He developed the "tatami-level" camera position — 30 cm off the ground, corresponding to the height of a person seated on a tatami mat. It did not gain a Western reputation until the 1970s; Ozu had died in 1963, never having lived to see his international recognition.

events.title: Pather Panchali Released
events.blurb: A first-time director shot a Bengali village drama across three years in fragments whenever he could afford to — including pawning his wife's jewellery to finish an opening sequence of a boy chasing a train through tall grass. It won a Humanist Prize at Cannes and launched a tradition of realist Indian cinema that bypassed Bombay entirely.
events.revealBlurb: August 26, 1955 — Satyajit Ray's debut. He was a commercial illustrator with no directing experience; the crew were mostly amateurs. The score was composed by an then-obscure sitarist named Ravi Shankar, recorded in a single 11-hour session. The West Bengal government funded its completion after seeing rough footage.

events.title: The Fellowship of the Ring Released
events.blurb: A New Zealand director released the first of three films shot simultaneously in his homeland adapting a mid-20th-century English fantasy novel. The ensemble cast and landscape cinematography, the 5,000 days of digital effects by a Wellington-based studio, and the willingness to treat the fantasy material completely seriously pulled the genre from ghetto to respectability. The trilogy's final instalment would win 11 Oscars.
events.revealBlurb: December 19, 2001 — Peter Jackson. The three films were shot over 438 days in New Zealand. Jackson's Weta Workshop became a world-leading effects house. The author's son Christopher Tolkien openly disliked the adaptations but inherited the royalty checks regardless.

events.title: Spirited Away Wins Oscar
events.blurb: A Japanese animated film about a 10-year-old girl's adventure in a bathhouse for spirits won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature, an unprecedented achievement for an Asian work in the category. The film's director, then 62, had been making animated features for decades, but most American audiences had never heard of him or his studio. The Oscar made the director a household name and put his studio's catalog on every arthouse wishlist.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 2003 — Hayao Miyazaki and Studio Ghibli's film won Best Animated Feature. Miyazaki did not attend the ceremony in protest of the Iraq War. "Spirited Away" remains Japan's highest-grossing film and grossed over $395 million worldwide.

events.title: Hippocratic Oath Composed
events.blurb: Greek medical writers associated with a physician teaching on an Aegean island composed a short ethical oath addressed to Apollo and Asclepius, binding physicians to care for their patients, respect their teachers, preserve patient confidences, and do no harm. The document is arguably the oldest surviving code of professional ethics. Modern versions, substantially modified, are still sworn by many medical-school graduates.
events.revealBlurb: c. 400 BCE — attributed to Hippocrates of Kos, though probably composed by his students or school. The modern "first, do no harm" is actually not in the original Greek text; it appears later in Hippocrates' Epidemics. The oath still shows up at white-coat ceremonies.

events.title: Snow's Cholera Pump
events.blurb: A London physician, investigating a cholera outbreak in a Soho neighbourhood that had killed 127 people in three days, mapped the cases and traced their common origin to a public water pump on Broad Street. He persuaded the local parish authorities to remove the pump's handle. New cases stopped almost immediately. His investigation established that cholera was a water-borne disease — against the reigning theory that it spread through "miasmas" in the air.
events.revealBlurb: September 8, 1854 — John Snow, Soho, London. His sketched map of the cases clustered around the pump is a founding document of epidemiology. The pump's water source had been contaminated by a nearby cesspit. A replica pump stands at the site today, with its handle symbolically removed.

events.title: Ross Identifies Malaria Vector
events.blurb: A 40-year-old British army medical officer working in colonial India dissected an Anopheles mosquito that had fed on a patient with malarial fever and observed the malaria parasite's oocysts developing in the mosquito's stomach wall. He had been pursuing the mosquito-borne hypothesis, championed by his mentor in London, for years. The discovery transformed tropical-disease prevention into an enterprise of draining swamps and destroying mosquito breeding sites.
events.revealBlurb: August 20, 1897 — Ronald Ross in Secunderabad, India. He called it his "mosquito day." Ross won the 1902 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. The mentor who had championed the mosquito hypothesis, Patrick Manson, was quietly robbed of credit at the time but is now recognized as a co-founder of tropical medicine.

events.title: Insulin Administered to a Patient
events.blurb: A 14-year-old diabetic patient near death at a Toronto hospital received an injection of pancreatic extract prepared by two medical researchers after earlier formulations had failed due to impurities. The boy recovered, and researchers moved ward to ward injecting the remaining diabetic patients — transforming a death sentence into a manageable condition within weeks.

events.title: Fleming Discovers Penicillin
events.blurb: A 47-year-old Scottish bacteriologist returning from a summer holiday to his London laboratory noticed that one of the staphylococcus-culture plates he had left stacked on his bench had been contaminated by a mold, and that a clear zone of inhibition around the mold showed the bacteria had died there. He identified the mold genus, isolated an anti-bacterial substance it produced, and published his findings — which were largely ignored for over a decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 28, 1928 — Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital, London. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford successfully purified penicillin in 1941, making it a usable drug. They shared the 1945 Nobel with Fleming. The drug's mass production during WWII saved hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers' lives.

events.title: Non-Cooperation Movement Launched
events.blurb: A lawyer who had spent two decades in South Africa returned to his homeland, assumed leadership of the Congress party, and launched the first mass civil-disobedience campaign against British rule. Millions boycotted British schools, courts, and textiles; bonfires of foreign cloth burned across the country. He called it off abruptly 18 months later after a mob burned 22 policemen alive at a northern village.
events.revealBlurb: August 1, 1920 — Mohandas Gandhi. Law practices and schools emptied. The student Jawaharlal Nehru came home from Cambridge to join. The suspension after Chauri Chaura was controversial; many activists thought Gandhi had thrown away momentum.

events.title: Indian Independence & Partition
events.blurb: At the stroke of midnight, two new independent dominions came into existence on the subcontinent — one majority-Hindu, one majority-Muslim — as the British flag was lowered on the largest and oldest of Britain's imperial possessions. The division of provinces along religious lines displaced between 10 and 20 million people, and perhaps a million died in the communal violence that followed.
events.revealBlurb: August 14-15, 1947 — Pakistan on the 14th, India on the 15th. The boundary lines had been drawn by a London barrister, Cyril Radcliffe, who had never visited the subcontinent and had 36 days to complete the task. Nehru's "Tryst with Destiny" speech was delivered at midnight from the Constituent Assembly.

events.title: Constitution of India Adopted
events.blurb: A constituent assembly of 299 members, chaired by a Bombay-trained lawyer from a once-"untouchable" community, completed two years and eleven months of debate to enact the longest written national constitution in the world — 395 articles, 22 parts, 8 schedules — establishing a secular, socialist, democratic republic. It came into force on the anniversary of a 1930 declaration of complete independence.
events.revealBlurb: January 26, 1950 — B.R. Ambedkar, chair of the drafting committee. The date — Republic Day — was chosen because it marked the 20th anniversary of Congress's Purna Swaraj declaration. The final handwritten copy is illuminated by the artist Nandalal Bose.

events.title: Indian Parliament Attack
events.blurb: Five gunmen in an SUV with a false government sticker drove past an outer cordon of the national legislature building in the capital, were challenged at a second checkpoint, and opened fire. They were shot dead in a 30-minute gun battle in the precinct gardens; nine security personnel were killed. The attack brought India and Pakistan to the brink of their fourth war; a million soldiers mobilized on both sides of the border.
events.revealBlurb: December 13, 2001 — the attackers were linked to Jaish-e-Mohammed and Lashkar-e-Taiba. Prime Minister Vajpayee and most MPs were inside the building at the time. The attack inspired the Indian terminology "Operation Parakram" for the massive military build-up that followed.

events.title: Chandrayaan-3 Lunar Landing
events.blurb: An Indian robotic spacecraft, after a 40-day journey that included a series of orbit-raising maneuvers to conserve fuel, performed a successful soft landing on the Moon's south polar region — a target no previous mission had reached. India became the fourth country to land on the Moon and the first to land in the south polar region, where water ice is believed to be preserved in permanently shadowed craters.
events.revealBlurb: August 23, 2023 — 18:04 IST. The lander was called Vikram; its rover was Pragyan. The national space agency ISRO had lost its predecessor Chandrayaan-2 at this phase four years earlier. The budget of the mission was around $75 million — less than the movie Interstellar.

events.title: Battles of Lexington and Concord
events.blurb: That spring morning, British regulars marching to seize a colonial weapons cache at Concord, Massachusetts, exchanged fire with local militia at Lexington before the colonists scattered; at Concord's North Bridge, a second volley triggered a running battle that chased the redcoats back to Boston. The day produced roughly 300 total casualties and the phrase "the shot heard round the world."
events.revealBlurb: April 19, 1775 — Lexington and Concord, Massachusetts. Nobody knows who fired first at Lexington — colonial accounts and British accounts flatly contradict each other. The phrase "shot heard round the world" was written by Ralph Waldo Emerson in 1837, over 60 years after the fact.

events.title: Storming of the Bastille
events.blurb: A mob of several thousand Parisians, enraged by the dismissal of a popular finance minister and rumours of royal military preparations, stormed a royal fortress prison on the city's eastern edge in search of gunpowder stored there. The garrison surrendered after a bloody four-hour assault; the commandant was murdered and his head carried on a pike through the streets. The prison itself held only seven prisoners. The date became the French national holiday.
