events.revealBlurb: July 14, 1789 — the Bastille. Seven prisoners: four forgers, two lunatics, one aristocrat imprisoned by his family. Marquis de Launay, the commandant, is the famous head on the pike. Parisians began demolishing the fortress the next morning; it was fully down within three months.

events.title: Declaration of the Rights of Man
events.blurb: The French National Constituent Assembly, meeting in a recently converted royal indoor tennis court, adopted a 17-article statement of universal rights: liberty, property, security, resistance to oppression, equality before the law, presumption of innocence, freedom of speech and religion. It did not grant women the vote or abolish slavery; revolutionaries would debate those extensions for years. It was still the most sweeping such declaration any European state had ever adopted.
events.revealBlurb: August 26, 1789 — a central drafter was the Marquis de Lafayette, the American Revolution veteran. The declaration was explicitly modeled on the U.S. Declaration of Independence; in fact, Jefferson, then in Paris as American minister, advised on its drafting. It remains part of France's constitutional law.

events.title: Haitian Revolution Begins
events.blurb: A voodoo ceremony in a wooded area of a French Caribbean sugar colony marked the coordinated signal for a mass uprising of enslaved Africans. Within ten days, plantations across the northern plain were in flames and 4,000 whites and mulattos were dead. It was the largest slave revolt in the history of the Americas and the only one that successfully established an independent state. The colony had been the richest in the Western hemisphere; it produced 40 percent of the world's sugar.
events.revealBlurb: August 22, 1791 — Saint-Domingue (now Haiti). The ceremony was at Bois Caïman, led by voodoo priest Dutty Boukman. Toussaint Louverture emerged as principal leader, though he was captured by the French in 1802 and died in a freezing French prison cell. Independence came on January 1, 1804.

events.title: Grito de Dolores
events.blurb: A 57-year-old Catholic priest in a rural Mexican town, learning that a conspiracy of criollo-elite revolutionaries had been uncovered, rang his church bell in the middle of the night to summon his parishioners and call for the overthrow of Spanish colonial rule. He led his ragged army of peasants and mestizos toward the capital; the colonial government crushed them within four months and he was shot. The rebellion he had started, though, continued for 11 more years.
events.revealBlurb: September 16, 1810 — Father Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla at Dolores, Guanajuato. The exact wording of his "grito" is not recorded. Hidalgo was captured in March 1811 and executed by firing squad on July 30, 1811. September 16 is Mexico's Independence Day; the President still rings the bell each year.

events.title: Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact
events.blurb: Two ideologically opposed dictatorships stunned the world by signing a non-aggression treaty after midnight in a capital city, including a secret clause dividing neighbouring countries into separate spheres of influence like cuts of a butchered animal. Every government in Europe recalculated its position by morning.
events.revealBlurb: Signed August 23, 1939 in Moscow. The secret protocol carved up Poland, Finland, the Baltic states, and Romania between Germany and the USSR — without telling any of those countries. Stalin was so pleased he personally opened champagne. The pact lasted exactly 22 months.

events.title: Japanese-American Internment
events.blurb: A presidential order authorised the forced removal of all people of a specific ethnic ancestry from the entire western coast of a country — regardless of citizenship — to inland camps surrounded by guard towers and barbed wire, without trial or individual evidence of wrongdoing. Roughly 122,000 people were displaced; two-thirds were native-born citizens.
events.revealBlurb: Executive Order 9066, signed February 19, 1942. The Supreme Court upheld it in 1944. In 1988, Congress formally apologised and paid $20,000 in reparations to each surviving detainee — roughly 82,000 people. A 2011 Department of Justice memo officially acknowledged the government's lawyers had hidden evidence of innocence from the original court.

events.title: Liberation of Paris
events.blurb: A city that had been under foreign occupation for four years erupted into street fighting as its own police force led an uprising, then fell into celebration as armoured columns rolled through its boulevards, the military governor surrendered, and a tall general delivered an emotional speech from the steps of a historic civic building to a vast and weeping crowd.
events.revealBlurb: August 25, 1944. German General Dietrich von Choltitz surrendered despite Hitler's repeated orders to destroy the city's bridges, monuments, and water system. Von Choltitz later claimed he had ignored the orders to preserve Paris; historians note he may simply have lacked the engineers and explosives. De Gaulle's famous speech began: "Paris! Paris outraged! Paris broken! Paris martyred! But Paris liberated!"

events.title: Execution of Mussolini
events.blurb: The founder of one of the 20th century's major fascist movements was captured hiding in a German military convoy while attempting to flee across a northern border, taken to a lakeside village by communist partisans, and shot 26 hours later — his body then transported to a major city and hung upside down at a petrol station for public display.
events.revealBlurb: April 28, 1945 — executed at Giulino di Mezzegra on Lake Como, two days before Hitler's death. Mussolini and his mistress Clara Petacci were shot, then driven to Milan and strung up by their heels at the Piazzale Loreto — the same square where partisan hostages had been publicly displayed by Fascists a year earlier.

events.title: Death of Hitler
events.blurb: The dictator who had triggered the continent's most destructive conflict, directed the murder of millions, and sworn never to be taken alive shot himself in a subterranean command centre beneath a capital city now surrounded by enemy armies, having married his companion the previous day and designated a naval admiral as his successor.
events.revealBlurb: April 30, 1945 — Hitler shot himself at approximately 3:30 PM in the Führerbunker; Eva Braun took cyanide. Their bodies were carried to the garden and burned. By explicit prior order, no intact corpse was to fall into enemy hands. Soviet forces found the remains eight days after the surrender; Stalin kept the truth of their forensic identification secret for decades.

events.title: Eruption of Vesuvius
events.blurb: A volcano on the Italian peninsula, dormant for centuries and believed extinct by the farmers whose vineyards clung to its slopes, erupted in a single day, burying two wealthy resort towns and their roughly 16,000 inhabitants under 6 metres of ash, pumice, and pyroclastic flow. The buried cities lay undiscovered for 1,700 years.
events.revealBlurb: August 24, 79 CE — Pompeii and Herculaneum, under Mount Vesuvius. Pliny the Younger watched from across the Bay of Naples and wrote the only eyewitness account. Volcanologists still classify massive plinian eruptions by his name.

events.title: Great Lisbon Earthquake
events.blurb: On the morning of a major Catholic holy day, a magnitude-9 earthquake struck off the Atlantic coast of a European capital while most residents were at Mass. The quake was followed within 40 minutes by a tsunami that rolled up the Tagus River, and a citywide fire that burned for five days. Roughly 40,000 of the city's 200,000 inhabitants died.
events.revealBlurb: November 1, 1755 — All Saints' Day in Lisbon. Voltaire wrote his anti-optimist poem about it, then Candide. The Portuguese prime minister, the Marquis of Pombal, supposedly asked "What now? We bury the dead and feed the living" and rebuilt the city on a grid.

events.title: Hindenburg Disaster
events.blurb: A German passenger airship, the largest aircraft ever flown, caught fire as it approached its mooring mast at a New Jersey naval air station, and was consumed in less than 40 seconds. 36 of the 97 people on board died, along with one ground crew member. A radio reporter's anguished live commentary — "Oh, the humanity!" — entered popular idiom.
events.revealBlurb: May 6, 1937 — Lakehurst, NJ. The reporter was Herbert Morrison; he was actually there to record for later broadcast and didn't expect to be on air. The disaster effectively killed the commercial airship industry overnight.

events.title: Hurricane Katrina
events.blurb: A Category 3 hurricane made landfall on the US Gulf Coast, driving a storm surge that overtopped and breached the levee system protecting a major port city lying largely below sea level. 80 percent of the city flooded; 1,392 people died. The chaotic federal response — images of thousands stranded on a sports stadium roof, bodies floating in water — inflicted lasting damage on the administration in power.
events.revealBlurb: August 29, 2005 — New Orleans, Louisiana. The Superdome housed 30,000 evacuees for five days in deteriorating conditions. The head of FEMA, Michael Brown, had previously run the International Arabian Horse Association; he resigned within two weeks.

events.title: Turkey-Syria Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck in the pre-dawn darkness along the fault separating the Anatolian and Arabian tectonic plates, followed nine hours later by a nearly equal-magnitude aftershock. Over 59,000 people died across southern Turkey and northern Syria; 1.5 million were left homeless. Shoddy building construction, exempted from code over years of amnesty laws, drew furious public blame.
events.revealBlurb: February 6, 2023 — epicenter near Gaziantep. The disaster reshaped the Turkish elections three months later; contractors who had benefited from construction amnesties were prosecuted. In Syria, ongoing civil war hampered aid delivery.

events.title: Tulsa Race Massacre
events.blurb: An armed white mob, deputized by local police and in some cases flown in biplanes to drop makeshift bombs, attacked an affluent Black neighborhood in an Oklahoma oil city nicknamed "Black Wall Street." Over 18 hours they burned 35 blocks of homes and businesses, killed an estimated 100 to 300 residents, and arrested 6,000 survivors. Nobody was ever prosecuted.
events.revealBlurb: May 31 to June 1, 1921 — Greenwood District, Tulsa. The massacre was scrubbed from local newspapers and school curricula for 75 years. A state commission finally investigated in 2001. Mass graves are still being exhumed.

events.title: Emmett Till Murdered
events.blurb: A 14-year-old Black boy visiting family in a rural Southern state was abducted from his great-uncle's home in the middle of the night, tortured, shot, and thrown into a river with a cotton-gin fan tied around his neck. His mother insisted on an open-casket funeral so the world could see what had been done to her son. Photographs of the mutilated body, published in Jet magazine, galvanized a generation.
events.revealBlurb: August 28, 1955 — Money, Mississippi. His accuser, Carolyn Bryant, admitted decades later she had lied about the encounter. Her husband and his half-brother were acquitted by an all-white jury, then sold their confession to Look magazine knowing they couldn't be retried.

events.title: Birmingham Children's Crusade
events.blurb: Over several days in a notoriously segregated Alabama steel city, more than a thousand Black schoolchildren — some as young as 6 — marched out of classes in organized protest. Police commissioner Bull Connor ordered fire hoses and attack dogs deployed against them. Photographs of a teenage boy lunged at by a German shepherd appeared on front pages across the world.
events.revealBlurb: May 2-5, 1963 — Birmingham, Alabama. King agreed to use children over the objections of many advisers; they were less vulnerable to losing jobs for protesting. Within weeks, the Kennedy administration introduced what became the Civil Rights Act.

events.title: Medgar Evers Assassinated
events.blurb: The NAACP's field secretary in a Southern state was shot in the back in his own driveway as he returned home at 12:30 AM from a meeting, carrying T-shirts that read "Jim Crow Must Go." He died in front of his wife and three children. His killer, a Ku Klux Klan member, was tried twice; both trials ended in hung juries with all-white panels. He walked free for 31 years.
events.revealBlurb: June 12, 1963 — Jackson, Mississippi. His killer, Byron De La Beckwith, was finally convicted in 1994 after new witnesses came forward. Medgar's widow Myrlie Evers-Williams spent decades pursuing the case; she later chaired the NAACP.

events.title: March on Washington
events.blurb: A quarter-million Americans — three-quarters Black, a quarter white — gathered between the Washington and Lincoln Memorials on the 100th anniversary summer of the Emancipation Proclamation to demand the passage of civil-rights legislation then stalled in Congress. The event's closing address, given on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, contained a phrase repeated in eight paragraphs: "I have a dream."
events.revealBlurb: August 28, 1963. MLK's prepared text did not contain "I have a dream" — Mahalia Jackson, behind him on the dais, shouted "Tell them about the dream, Martin!" and he ad-libbed the most famous passage. The Justice Department had 4,000 troops on standby in case of violence. None was needed.

events.title: U.S. Constitution Ratified
events.blurb: New Hampshire became the ninth state to ratify the proposed Constitution, providing the three-fourths supermajority required to bring the new framework of government into effect and replace the faltering Articles of Confederation. The document created a federal republic with three separated branches of power — a design that had no exact precedent in world history.
events.revealBlurb: June 21, 1788 — New Hampshire. Rhode Island didn't ratify until May 1790 — over a year after the government had already begun operating. North Carolina waited until November 1789, after the First Congress had already convened.

events.title: Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire
events.blurb: A fire that broke out in a garment factory occupying the top three floors of a ten-story building in Manhattan's Greenwich Village killed 146 workers — mostly young immigrant women — in less than 18 minutes. Many died because exit doors had been locked from the outside; dozens jumped from the eighth, ninth, and tenth floors to their deaths on the sidewalk below, in full view of horrified onlookers.
events.revealBlurb: March 25, 1911 — Washington Place, New York City. The factory owners were indicted for manslaughter and acquitted, then collected on inflated insurance claims. The disaster triggered passage of more than 30 new labor safety laws in New York State.

events.title: Women's Suffrage Amendment Certified
events.blurb: The U.S. Secretary of State certified the ratification of the Nineteenth Amendment, prohibiting any state from denying the right to vote on account of sex. The amendment's passage followed a 72-year organised campaign that had begun at the Seneca Falls Convention in 1848, when most of its original signatories were ridiculed for the demand.

events.title: Apollo 1 Launchpad Fire
events.blurb: During a ground test at Cape Kennedy that afternoon, a fire broke out inside the Apollo 1 command module, killing all three crew members — Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee — in less than a minute. The cause was an electrical spark in an atmosphere of pure oxygen at elevated pressure, and the hatch could not be opened quickly enough to save anyone.
events.revealBlurb: January 27, 1967 — Launch Complex 34, Cape Kennedy, Florida. The crew could not escape because the hatch required 90 seconds to open inward — and the fire created pressure that made it impossible to swing. The disaster set the Moon program back 20 months but ultimately produced a safer spacecraft.

events.title: Bush v. Gore Halts Florida Recount
events.blurb: The Supreme Court ruled 5–4 to halt the manual recount of Florida's contested presidential ballots, effectively awarding the state's 25 electoral votes to Republican George W. Bush and deciding the closest presidential election since 1876. The margin in Florida's certified count was 537 votes out of nearly 6 million cast; Al Gore ultimately conceded, and Bush won the presidency 271–266 in the Electoral College.
events.revealBlurb: December 12, 2000 — Washington, D.C. The per curiam opinion included the extraordinary disclaimer that the ruling "is limited to the present circumstances" and should not be treated as precedent. The butterfly ballot design in Palm Beach County alone may have cost Gore 2,000–3,000 votes to Pat Buchanan.

events.title: Great Fire of London
events.blurb: A blaze beginning in a baker's shop on Pudding Lane burned for four days, destroying 373 acres of the medieval city including 13,200 houses, 87 churches, and most civic buildings. The fire melted the lead roof of St. Paul's Cathedral and was visible 60 miles away, yet officially killed only six people due to rapid evacuation before the flames spread.

events.title: Krakatoa Eruption
events.blurb: An island volcano in the strait between two large Indonesian islands exploded in a series of detonations culminating in a final blast so loud it was heard 4,800 kilometres away and circled the planet four times as a pressure wave. The eruption generated tsunamis that killed 36,000 people on surrounding coasts; the resulting atmospheric dust produced red-green sunsets worldwide for years.
events.revealBlurb: August 27, 1883 — Krakatoa, Sunda Strait. The final explosion had an acoustic energy roughly equivalent to 200 megatons of TNT. The glow of the afterburn may be what Edvard Munch painted in The Scream a decade later.

events.title: Mexico City Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 8.0 earthquake off the Pacific coast of Mexico sent seismic waves 350 kilometres inland to the capital, where the soft lake-bed soil beneath the city amplified the shaking for four full minutes. Around 400 buildings collapsed and at least 10,000 people died. The slow, corruption-tainted government response discredited the ruling party and helped end its 70-year monopoly on power.
events.revealBlurb: September 19, 1985 — Mexico City. Thirty-two years later to the day — September 19, 2017 — another major earthquake hit the same city. The coincidence is eerie but not mystical: the annual national earthquake drill was held that morning to mark 1985.

events.title: Nepal Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck central Nepal, flattening villages in the mountainous countryside, damaging UNESCO-listed temples in the capital, and triggering avalanches that killed 22 climbers at Mount Everest base camp. The final death toll approached 9,000. Much of the historic royal square in Kathmandu was reduced to rubble.
events.revealBlurb: April 25, 2015 — Gorkha district. The quake moved Mount Everest about 3 centimetres southwest and rose Kathmandu by 1 metre. A 16-year-old boy was pulled alive from a collapsed building five days later.

events.title: COVID-19 Pandemic Declared
events.blurb: The World Health Organization, having watched a novel coronavirus spread from a single city to 114 countries in ten weeks, formally upgraded its assessment from epidemic to pandemic. Within days, much of the world entered some form of lockdown — schools shut, flights grounded, stock markets crashed. Before vaccines arrived a year later, it would kill millions.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 2020 — WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. The first known case had been reported in Wuhan in early December 2019. Official global death toll exceeded 7 million; excess mortality studies suggest the real number is closer to 20 million.

events.title: Battle of Actium
events.blurb: Off the coast of northwestern Greece, Octavian's fleet under Marcus Agrippa met the combined ships of Mark Antony and Cleopatra. When Cleopatra's Egyptian squadron broke off and fled mid-battle, Antony abandoned his own fleet to follow her; his 19 legions on shore surrendered a week later. The last serious rival to a single ruler of Rome was gone.
events.revealBlurb: September 2, 31 BCE. Antony and Cleopatra escaped to Alexandria, where both committed suicide the following year — Antony by falling on his sword (badly), Cleopatra by asp bite (legend) or poison. Octavian kept Cleopatra's son Caesarion alive just long enough to read Caesar's will, then had him killed.

events.title: Beginning of the Crisis of the Third Century
events.blurb: The assassination of Emperor Severus Alexander by his own troops triggered nearly fifty years of catastrophic instability: more than twenty emperors in half a century, nearly all killed by soldiers or rivals, with simultaneous invasions across every frontier and a fragmenting empire that briefly split into three competing states. The population and economy contracted severely.
events.revealBlurb: 235 CE, Germany. Maximinus Thrax, the soldier who replaced Severus Alexander, was reportedly 8 feet tall and drank a wheelbarrow's worth of water per day — details that are almost certainly exaggerated. He never visited Rome during his three-year reign and was killed by his own troops outside Aquileia.

events.title: Diocletian's Tetrarchy
events.blurb: Recognising that one man could not govern and defend an empire stretching from Scotland to Mesopotamia, Emperor Diocletian formalised a system of four co-rulers — two senior Augusti and two junior Caesars — each commanding a quarter of the empire from a frontier capital. He also doubled the size of the army, reformed the tax system, and set maximum prices for hundreds of goods.
events.revealBlurb: 293 CE. Diocletian is the only Roman emperor to voluntarily abdicate and retire — he went to grow cabbages in his palace at Split (modern Croatia). When colleagues urged him to return, he reportedly replied that if they could see the cabbages he had grown, they would not ask.

events.title: Julian the Apostate's Pagan Revival
events.blurb: Emperor Julian — Constantine's nephew, raised as a Christian — publicly renounced Christianity upon taking power, reopened pagan temples that had been confiscated or closed, restored their revenues, and barred Christians from teaching classical literature in schools. He lasted only eighteen months before dying from a spear wound during a Persian campaign.
events.revealBlurb: November 361 CE. Julian wrote philosophical treatises, got up before dawn to perform sacrifices, and reportedly sacrificed so many oxen that soldiers nicknamed him "the Slaughterhouse." His pagan restoration died with him; every successor returned to Christianity.

events.title: Deposition of Romulus Augustulus
events.blurb: The Germanic warlord Odoacer deposed the sixteen-year-old emperor Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna — a boy whose mocking nickname meant "Little Augustus" — and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople, informing the eastern emperor that the west no longer needed a separate ruler. Odoacer spared Romulus's life, finding him too young and too minor to bother executing, and exiled him to a villa in Campania on a pension.
events.revealBlurb: September 4, 476 CE. The last western emperor's name combined the city's legendary founder and its first emperor — an irony Roman writers noticed immediately. Contemporaries did not regard this moment as "the fall of Rome"; that framing came centuries later. The eastern empire in Constantinople continued for another 977 years.

events.title: San Francisco Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.9 earthquake ripped a 477-kilometre tear through the fault running up the California coast, hitting a West Coast boom city just after 5 AM. The shaking was severe, but the four-day fire that followed — fed by broken gas mains and fought with limited water from shattered pipes — did most of the damage, destroying 80 percent of the city and killing around 3,000.
events.revealBlurb: April 18, 1906 — San Francisco. The mayor authorized dynamiting buildings to create firebreaks; most of the dynamiting actually spread the fire. The opera singer Enrico Caruso, in town for a performance, vowed never to return. He didn't.

events.title: Great Kantō Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.9 earthquake struck the main Japanese island at noon, as hundreds of thousands of households were preparing lunch over charcoal braziers. The fires that erupted in the collapsed wooden city were fanned by a typhoon passing offshore, merging into a single firestorm with tornadoes of flame. Around 140,000 people died; 1.9 million were left homeless.
events.revealBlurb: September 1, 1923 — Tokyo and Yokohama. A persistent false rumor that ethnic Koreans were poisoning wells led to vigilante massacres of some 6,000 Korean residents. September 1 is now Japan's Disaster Prevention Day.

events.title: 1931 China Floods
events.blurb: A succession of heavy snowmelt and monsoon rains caused the three great rivers of central China to breach their banks simultaneously, flooding 180,000 square kilometres of farmland and cities. Estimates of the death toll range from 500,000 to 4 million; much of the toll came from subsequent famine and water-borne disease. It is likely the deadliest non-pandemic natural disaster in recorded history.
events.revealBlurb: July-November 1931 — Yangtze, Yellow, and Huai rivers. Wuhan was submerged for months. A young Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist government was blamed for the weak response; flood relief was a major propaganda opportunity for the Communists in Jiangxi.

events.title: Hurricane Andrew
events.blurb: A compact Category 5 hurricane made landfall in southern Florida in the early hours of a late summer morning, its eyewall gusts reaching 280 km/h. It destroyed 63,500 houses, left 175,000 people homeless, and caused $27 billion in damage — then the costliest natural disaster in US history. Building codes across the Florida peninsula were rewritten as a direct consequence.
events.revealBlurb: August 24, 1992 — Homestead, Florida. It was the first named storm of an otherwise quiet season. Eleven insurance companies went bankrupt settling claims. For comparison, Katrina 13 years later cost over $100 billion.

events.title: Indian Ocean Tsunami
events.blurb: A magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off the western coast of Sumatra — the third-largest ever recorded — displaced so much water that tsunami waves up to 30 metres high raced across the Indian Ocean, hitting 14 countries within hours. Around 228,000 people died in Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India, Thailand, and as far away as Somalia. No warning system existed.
events.revealBlurb: December 26, 2004 — Boxing Day. A 10-year-old British girl named Tilly Smith recognized the receding tide from a school geography lesson and got her family's Phuket beach evacuated, saving around 100 lives. A basin-wide warning system was operational by 2006.

events.title: Brunelleschi's Dome Completed
events.blurb: A Florentine goldsmith turned architect completed, after 16 years of work without scaffolding, a vast octagonal dome over the crossing of a century-old cathedral. The double-shelled design, assembled with four million bricks in a self-supporting herringbone pattern, spanned 42 metres — wider than any dome built since Roman antiquity. The cathedral had stood domeless for over a century, waiting for someone to figure out how.
events.revealBlurb: August 25, 1436 — consecrated. Filippo Brunelleschi at Santa Maria del Fiore, Florence. He refused to leave blueprints, fearing competitors would steal the ideas. Part of the technique was rediscovered only in the 20th century through forensic study of the bricks.

events.title: Erasmus Publishes Praise of Folly
events.blurb: A 44-year-old Dutch humanist scholar, passing a week at the London home of his friend Thomas More, dashed off a satirical essay in Latin in which a personified Folly delivered a self-congratulatory oration cataloguing the foolishnesses of every social station — pedantic scholars, superstitious monks, greedy merchants, bloody princes. The essay circulated across Europe in pirated editions within months; it would be read as a scathing critique of the corrupt Catholic Church.
events.revealBlurb: 1511 — Desiderius Erasmus. The pun of the title is trilingual: "Moriae Encomium" in Latin, pointing at Thomas More (Morus) as well as at folly. It was placed on the Papal Index of Prohibited Books in 1559. More, who thought the essay funny, was canonized after being beheaded by Henry VIII.

events.title: Luther Posts the 95 Theses
events.blurb: A 33-year-old German university theologian sent his local archbishop a letter enclosing a 95-point list of academic propositions challenging the papal indulgence system — the practice of selling forgiveness of sins. By tradition, he also posted the Latin theses on the door of his university church, which served as a community bulletin board. Copies reached print within weeks and spread across Germany. He had intended academic debate; he ignited the Protestant Reformation.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1517 — Martin Luther at Wittenberg Castle Church. Most scholars doubt the physical nailing-to-the-door story; the letter to Archbishop Albrecht of Mainz is well-documented. October 31 is now celebrated as Reformation Day in many Protestant countries.

events.title: First Circumnavigation Complete
events.blurb: The last seaworthy ship of a Spanish expedition that had set out three years earlier with five vessels dropped anchor in the Guadalquivir River in Spain — the first ship ever to return to its port of departure after sailing completely around the world. Of the 270 men who had departed, 18 returned alive. Its captain, though no longer the expedition's original commander — who had been killed in the Philippines — had personally sailed the ship the entire way home.
events.revealBlurb: September 6, 1522 — Juan Sebastián Elcano aboard the Victoria. The voyage proved the earth was circumnavigable, and also forced the first adjustment of the ship's log by a day (a precursor to the concept of the International Date Line). Elcano himself died at sea in 1526, three ships into another expedition.

events.title: Galileo's Telescope Observations
events.blurb: A 46-year-old Paduan university mathematics professor, having improved the magnification of a newly invented Dutch optical toy from 3x to 30x, pointed his telescope at the night sky. Over the following months he observed craters on the moon, four previously unknown moons circling Jupiter, phases of Venus, and individual stars resolvable in the milky white band of the Milky Way. His findings, published in a short Latin book, transformed astronomy.
events.revealBlurb: January 7, 1610 — Galileo Galilei observed Jupiter's moons from Padua. His book "Sidereus Nuncius" (The Starry Messenger) was rushed into print in March. The phases of Venus, observed later that year, were decisive evidence against the Ptolemaic earth-centered model.

events.title: Madonna's "Like a Prayer" Video
events.blurb: The music video for a 30-year-old singer's new single, featuring burning crosses, stigmata, and the singer kissing a Black saint statue coming to life, premiered during a Pepsi commercial at the start of a television special paid for by the soft-drink company. The Vatican condemned the video as blasphemous; conservative Christian groups organized boycotts; Pepsi paid the singer $5 million to sever their sponsorship deal. Her album sold 15 million copies.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 1989 — the Pepsi commercial; the full video premiered on MTV March 3. Director Mary Lambert. The controversy gave Madonna an estimated $5 million for the Pepsi deal plus enormous free publicity; she kept the money. The album "Like a Prayer" remains her best-reviewed.

events.title: The Simpsons Premieres
events.blurb: A half-hour animated primetime sitcom about a dysfunctional yellow-skinned family in the fictional American town of Springfield premiered as a Christmas special on a fledgling US television network. The show's acerbic satire, cartoon slapstick, and unprecedented crossover appeal — with children and adults watching together — established animation as a legitimate prime-time format. It is still in production three and a half decades later, the longest-running American scripted prime-time TV series.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1989 — the Christmas special "Simpsons Roasting on an Open Fire" on the Fox network. Created by Matt Groening from shorts he had been making for The Tracey Ullman Show since 1987. The family was named after Groening's own family except Bart, an anagram of "brat."

events.title: Tamagotchi Released
events.blurb: A Japanese toy company released a small egg-shaped plastic keychain with a tiny LCD screen and three buttons. The device simulated a virtual pet that needed feeding, playing with, and cleaning up after — with beeps demanding attention at all hours, including in the middle of lessons in schools. Schools banned them. 40 million units sold globally. The craze prefigured the attention-hijacking mobile apps of decades later.
events.revealBlurb: November 23, 1996 — Bandai. Designed by Akihiro Yokoi and Aki Maita. Later versions could be put to sleep or paused; the original would simply "die" if neglected, and the keychain had to be reset. The name combines Japanese "tamago" (egg) and "watch."

events.title: Princess Diana Dies
events.blurb: A 36-year-old former British princess and two others died in a high-speed car crash in an underpass in central Paris after their driver attempted to evade pursuing paparazzi. Her death — ten months after her divorce from the heir to the British throne — triggered a massive public outpouring of grief that caught the British monarchy off guard. Over a million bouquets of flowers were left at London's royal palaces. Her funeral a week later was watched by 2.5 billion people globally.
events.revealBlurb: August 31, 1997 — Diana, Princess of Wales at the Pont de l'Alma tunnel. Her companion Dodi Fayed and the drunk driver Henri Paul also died; bodyguard Trevor Rees-Jones survived. Elton John performed a rewritten "Candle in the Wind" at the funeral, which became the best-selling single of all time.

events.title: South Park Premieres
events.blurb: An animated half-hour adult-comedy series about four foul-mouthed 8-year-old boys in a small Colorado mountain town premiered on the Comedy Central cable network. The deliberately crude cut-paper animation style and its topical-to-the-minute production timeline (each episode was produced in a week rather than the months typical for animation) gave it a reactive speed no other animated show could match. It would remain in production for over 25 years.
events.revealBlurb: August 13, 1997 — created by Trey Parker and Matt Stone. Their earlier Christmas short, "The Spirit of Christmas," had circulated as a VHS among Hollywood executives in 1995. The show's 1999 feature film nearly received an NC-17 rating; the MPAA gave it R after the creators submitted it six times.
